samples.text:
The pie chart shows the sources of electricity in a country in 2024 and the line graph shows the price of electricity for households and businesses from 2016 to 2024.

In the pie chart, natural gas was the biggest source with 38%. Wind was the second with 27% and nuclear was 14%. The other sources was smaller, biomass had 9%, solar had 7%, other had 3% and coal was only 2%.

In the line graph, households always paid more than businesses. In 2016 the price for households was 15 cents per kWh and for businesses 11 cents. From 2016 to 2020 the prices increased slowly and households reached 17 cents and businesses 12 cents. Then in 2022 the prices increased very sharply, households price doubled to 34 cents and business price was 29 cents. After that, both prices goes down in 2024, to 27 cents for households and 21 cents for businesses.

Overall, gas and wind produced most of the electricity, and the price of electricity rose a lot in 2022 and then fell but it was still higher than 2016.
samples.why: Overview present but placed at the end · both visuals covered with accurate figures · mechanical organisation and linking · limited range of vocabulary · comma splices and agreement errors that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
The pie chart illustrates the proportion of a country's electricity produced from different sources in 2024, and the line graph shows how average electricity prices for homes and businesses changed between 2016 and 2024.

Overall, natural gas and wind together generated almost two thirds of the country's electricity. As for prices, both groups saw a dramatic rise in 2022, followed by a partial fall, with households paying more than businesses throughout.

Natural gas was the largest source of electricity, at 38%, followed by wind at 27%. Nuclear power contributed 14%, while biomass and solar provides 9% and 7% respectively. Coal played only a very minor role, accounting for just 2%, and other sources made up the remaining 3%.

Turning to prices, households paid 15 cents per kWh in 2016, compared with 11 cents for businesses. These figures rose only marginally over the next four years, to 17 and 12 cents. However, between 2020 and 2022 prices doubled for households, reaching 34 cents, and more than doubled for businesses, which were charged 29 cents. By 2024 prices had dropped back to 27 cents for households and 21 cents for businesses, but this was still well above the 2016 levels.
samples.why: Clear overview of generation mix and price trend · key features highlighted with apt comparisons · logical paragraphing and good linking · some less common vocabulary (marginally) · one minor agreement slip.

samples.text:
The pie chart breaks down electricity generation in one country by source in 2024, while the line graph tracks the average price of electricity paid by households and businesses from 2016 to 2024.

Natural gas and wind power dominated the generation mix, whereas coal had become almost negligible. Prices for both types of consumer were broadly stable until 2020 before spiking sharply, and although they eased by 2024, they remained far higher than at the start of the period.

Natural gas supplied the largest share of electricity, at 38%, with wind not far behind at 27%. Nuclear power contributed a further 14%, while biomass and solar accounted for 9% and 7% respectively. Coal generated a mere 2%, even less than the 3% from other sources.

Households consistently paid more per unit than businesses. Between 2016 and 2020, household prices crept up from 15 to 17 cents per kWh and business prices from 11 to 12 cents. Over the following two years, however, the household price doubled to 34 cents, and the business price more than doubled to 29 cents. By 2024 they had fallen back to 27 and 21 cents respectively, still 12 and 10 cents higher than in 2016.
samples.why: Skilful overview of both visuals · data grouped logically with precise derived comparisons · cohesion well managed · natural, precise vocabulary (negligible, crept up, eased) · wide range of structures with no errors.
